Position error after a visual gap

Mean position error for fresh versus older visual measurements. Each column includes the available tracks in that age group. The distance filter uses the server's true distance from the observer to the target at that cycle.

Position error for one sample
√[(xWM − xtruth)² + (yWM − ytruth)²]
WM is the agent’s world-model position for the target. Truth is the server’s fullstate position for that same target and cycle. For example, errors of 0.30 m in x and 0.40 m in y give a position error of 0.50 m.

Mean in each table cell = sum of those position errors ÷ number of measured samples for that target group and visual age.

Self localization

Fresh visual position is where the agent thinks it is based on what it just saw, such as flags and field lines. Fresh visual looking direction is where it thinks it is looking, in degrees. Both are measured before librcsc updates the world model. The paired tables compare the fresh visual and world-model estimates on the same cycles.

How self-position error can affect a 2.7 m/cycle kick

The server uses the true ball-to-player distance and angle to apply the kick. Helios chooses its power using the estimated distance and angle.

Kick rate = player kick power rate × (1 − 0.25 × |ball angle from body| ÷ 180° − 0.25 × surface gap ÷ kickable margin). Surface gap is center-to-center distance minus the player and ball radii.

Requested power = needed change in ball velocity ÷ estimated kick rate. Applied acceleration = requested power × true kick rate in the kick direction, before server noise and limits.

If the self-position error changes the estimated distance to the ball

Take a type-0 player with the ball 0.65 m straight ahead and already rolling toward the target at 0.50 m/cycle. A first-step speed of 2.70 m/cycle needs a 2.20 m/cycle velocity increase. Suppose the ball’s estimated field position is correct, and the entire 4.31 cm self-position error makes the player think the ball is farther away. Helios then asks for too much power.

Overestimate of ball distanceKick powerFirst-step speed (m/cycle)Speed error (m/cycle)
4.31 cm91.562.738+0.038
Half (2.155 cm)90.772.719+0.019
0 cm90.002.700+0.000

In this example, halving the distance error cuts the speed error from about 0.038 to 0.019 m/cycle. Speeds are for the ball’s first movement, before decay.

If the estimated player and ball positions shift together

A fresh visual ball position can inherit the same field-position shift as the player. The player-to-ball offset then stays the same, so this shift does not change the kick rate. Aiming at a fixed field target can still change. With a sideways shift of 4.31 cm and a target 20 m away, the aim changes by about 0.12°, or 0.58 cm sideways in the first cycle at 2.70 m/cycle. Halving the shift reduces that to about 0.29 cm.

These examples isolate position error and assume correct ball velocity and body angle. The 4.31 cm input is the overall exp1 self-position mean. Actual kicks also depend on ball and body-angle estimates, server noise, and speed and power limits.

Code references. rcssserver Player::kick and MPObject::_inc, librcsc PlayerType::kickRate and WorldModel::localizeBall, and Helios Body_KickOneStep::execute.

Where the world-model bar is higher, check how the player observation was assigned to a track before changing the sensor model. This comparison can reflect both player matching and fusion. Position and velocity use separate sets of paired samples.

How much does seeing the same target again help?

The gap between the lines shows how much the estimate changed when the target came back into view. It shows where a model that predicts through missed observations has room to help.

How often each view gives an update and sees a target

Visual age counts cycles since the last visual position update. A track’s position count can reset after hearing.

When does hearing help?

Compare the decoded position in a teammate message with the receiver’s local estimate. The report calls it better or worse when the two errors differ by more than 5 cm. Both are scored against the same fullstate position.

  • Seen now. Compare with the receiver’s fresh visual position, before fusion. Player identity must be visible for this comparison.
  • Unseen. Compare the message with the ball forecast made on the preceding cycle, or with the previous position of an identified player carried forward one cycle.

Which message types carry useful positions?

Lower decoded error means the payload itself was closer to fullstate. The last two columns show how often it beat or lost to the local reference by over 5 cm. The rest were within 5 cm. When is a heard position more likely to be worse?
Do the final tracks with fresh reports also look better?

These results test what would happen if you chose the reported position over the stated reference. Earlier messages can already be part of that reference. To measure the effect of the actual fusion rule, log the same-cycle estimate immediately before and after applying the message. Use S0 to measure the overall effect of communication on the run.

Predicted state versus the real next cycle

The prediction is scored against fullstate exactly one cycle later. The carry-forward baseline uses the current estimate on the same samples. Compare the ball velocity and position rows to see which the current motion model helps more.

When does predicting the ball beat carrying its estimate forward?

Schema v2 supplies numeric next-cycle predictions for self position and body angle and for ball position and velocity. It does not log next self velocity or next opponent/teammate state.

What to test next

  • Tracking through visual gaps. Use the before-and-after reacquisition plot to choose ages and targets for a prediction model. V1 tests the combined benefit of a wider cone and a see every cycle. Separate cone and update-rate experiments are needed to distinguish their effects.
  • Player matching and missing fields. Where a fresh player estimate is better than its final track, test F1 for identity and F2 for the additional motion and orientation fields. Compare position error and track availability together.
  • Teammate fusion. Run S0 against the baseline and compare stale tracks within the same distance and age ranges. Log before and after heard updates to see which messages help.
  • Fresh measurement correction. Use N1 to isolate distance noise where the raw distance plot shows the biggest errors. Direction and motion-field rounding remain.

How to read the results

The report uses play_on samples with valid fullstate and gives every eligible sample equal weight. Grouped plots omit groups with fewer than 100 measurements. The detailed CSV includes sample counts, availability and additional breakdowns.

Dataset and calculation details

Source /home/nader/workspace/denoise/logs/exp1. Self uses one row per observer decision. Ball and players use one row per observer, on-field object and decision. Missing measurements are excluded from the error average. Means use absolute or Euclidean errors, and percentiles are approximate. Distance bins include the lower bound and exclude the upper bound.

Raw player errors exclude ambiguous nearest-direction matches. Fused track results can include heuristic nearest-truth associations. Ground-truth bins are for evaluation. Train with features the agent can access and evaluate on held-out games.
